lead: A smart sensor is a complete measuring chain on one chip or module. The sensing element, an amplifier and filter, an analog-to-digital converter, a small processor and a digital bus sit together. Memory inside holds the calibration coefficients. The output is already in engineering units, addressed, and often checked against an internal reference. You meet these in a phone's pressure and humidity sensors, in a car's manifold pressure sensor, and in a factory transmitter that reports over a bus. The point is to move calibration and correction close to the signal, before noise and cable loss spoil it.
prereq: You need: the signal-conditioning chain from Unit 6 (amplifiers, filters, data acquisition) and the micro sensor being made smart in 5.5.

blocks.text: The sensing element converts the measurand into a small voltage, current, resistance or capacitance. The amplifier raises this signal above the noise of the next stage, and the filter removes interference outside the band of interest. The ADC turns the conditioned analog voltage into a number. A 12-bit ADC with a 3.3 V reference has 2¹² = 4096 codes, so one code is 3.3 V / 4096 = 0.806 mV. That is resolution at the ADC pin, not the accuracy of the sensor.

A microcontroller (µC) or digital signal processor (DSP) reads the ADC count. Memory beside it holds the calibration coefficients: zero offset, span gain, linearity curve and temperature coefficients. The processor applies these, attaches the unit and sends the result on a digital bus. The memory is what makes the chain smart. Without it the processor has no record of what the element's 10 mV/kPa means, or how that sensitivity falls when the silicon warms.

The order matters. Correction after the ADC cannot recover a signal that clipped the amplifier or sat in the ADC's noise. The analog front end must keep the signal inside the converter's range over the whole operating temperature and supply range. The processor then works on clean numbers.
The processor runs a fixed sequence at every sample. Some syllabi call this the smart-sensor function list.

items: Linearisation maps the raw count to the measurand with a polynomial or lookup table. The table is written at factory calibration.
Offset and gain correction subtract the zero count and scale the span. A pressure sensor that reads 12 counts at 0 kPa has that 12 subtracted.
Temperature compensation uses an on-chip temperature sensor. Piezoresistive sensitivity falls with temperature, so the processor multiplies by a correction factor.
Autoranging changes the amplifier gain when the signal is small or near full scale, keeping the ADC on its useful bits.
Self-calibration switches an internal reference voltage or precision resistor to the input and checks the reading. It corrects gain drift, not a cracked diaphragm.
Self-diagnosis watches for open circuit, short circuit, overrange and a stuck output, and sets a fault flag in the status byte.
The output is a number with a unit, for example 101.3 kPa, not a bare ADC count.

blocks.text: Each function uses memory and code, so the same silicon element can be sold as a raw micro sensor or as a calibrated smart sensor. The calibrated version costs more because of test time, not because the diaphragm is different.

sections.h3: Buses, standards and the accuracy budget

blocks.text: IEEE 1451 defines a Transducer Electronic Data Sheet (TEDS). TEDS is a small memory block that gives the sensor's identity, range, calibration date and coefficients, so a network can read a new sensor and configure itself. The physical link can be I²C or SPI inside a board, UART for a short cable, CAN in a vehicle, or the 4–20 mA current loop with HART digital data superimposed on the same two wires. The 4–20 mA loop carries the measurement as a current; HART adds a low-level digital signal on top without disturbing the current.

A smart sensor carries its own processing and digital interface at chip or module level. An intelligent instrument is a complete panel meter or analyser that may use a smart sensor inside but adds display, keypad and enclosure. The distinction is packaging and scope, not intelligence in the everyday sense.

Do not quote the 12 bits as accuracy. Bits fix resolution; offset, gain error, nonlinearity, hysteresis and drift fix accuracy until calibration is applied. A 12-bit output can still be 2 % wrong if the ADC reference is wrong or the amplifier offset drifts. The resolution and accuracy budget must list each error source separately: sensor, amplifier, reference, ADC and calibration uncertainty.

examples.question: A piezoresistive pressure sensor has a sensitivity of 10 mV/kPa. Its amplifier has a voltage gain of 100 and drives a 12-bit ADC with a 3.3 V reference. Find (a) the ADC step size in mV, (b) the input-referred step in µV, and (c) the pressure change represented by one least significant bit in Pa.
steps: The ADC full-scale span is 3.3 V = 3300 mV.
A 12-bit ADC has 2¹² = 4096 codes. One step is Q = 3300 mV / 4096 = 0.805664 mV ≈ 0.806 mV.
Referred to the amplifier input, divide by the gain 100: 0.805664 mV / 100 = 0.00805664 mV = 8.05664 µV ≈ 8.06 µV.
The sensor sensitivity is 10 mV/kPa. Since 1 kPa = 1000 Pa, this is 10 mV / 1000 Pa = 0.01 mV/Pa = 10 µV/Pa.
Pressure per LSB = 8.05664 µV / (10 µV/Pa) = 0.805664 Pa ≈ 0.806 Pa.
examples.answer: One LSB represents 0.806 Pa, which is 8.06 µV at the sensor input and 0.806 mV at the ADC.
examples.check:
Vref = 3.3
N = 12
gain = 100.0
sens_mV_per_kPa = 10.0
Q_mV = Vref * 1000.0 / (2 ** N)
Q_in_uV = Q_mV * 1000.0 / gain
sens_uV_per_Pa = sens_mV_per_kPa * 1000.0 / 1000.0
Pa_per_LSB = Q_in_uV / sens_uV_per_Pa
print(round(Q_mV, 3))
print(round(Q_in_uV, 2))
print(round(Pa_per_LSB, 3))

traps: Quoting the ADC's 12 bits as the sensor accuracy. Bits give resolution only; offset, gain error and drift set accuracy until calibration.
Forgetting the amplifier gain when referring the LSB to the sensor input. A 0.806 mV ADC step is only 8.06 µV at the element.
Mixing kPa and Pa. A sensitivity of 10 mV/kPa is 10 µV/Pa, not 10 mV/Pa.
Assuming a digital bus removes analog error. The ADC reference, amplifier offset and sensor drift are still analog errors.
Calling every digital transmitter an intelligent instrument. A smart sensor is the chip or module with its own processing; an instrument adds display and enclosure.

quiz.q: What does TEDS stand for, and what does it hold?
quiz.a: Transducer Electronic Data Sheet. It holds the sensor identity, range, calibration date and calibration coefficients so a network can read and configure the device.

quiz.q: Why is memory needed inside a smart sensor?
quiz.a: Memory stores the zero offset, gain, linearity table, temperature coefficients and TEDS. The processor needs these to convert the raw ADC count into a calibrated value in engineering units without an external computer.

quiz.q: A sensor has sensitivity 20 mV/kPa, amplifier gain 50, and a 10-bit ADC with a 5 V reference. Find the pressure change represented by one LSB in Pa.
quiz.a: LSB at ADC = 5 V / 2¹⁰ = 5 V / 1024 = 4.8828 mV. Input-referred = 4.8828 mV / 50 = 0.097656 mV = 97.656 µV. Sensitivity = 20 mV/kPa = 20 µV/Pa. Pressure per LSB = 97.656 µV / 20 µV/Pa = 4.88 Pa.

quiz.q: A 16-bit ADC gives finer resolution than a 12-bit ADC. Does that prove the smart sensor is more accurate? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Sixteen bits divide the reference into 65,536 codes instead of 4096, so resolution is finer by 16 times. Accuracy still depends on the reference, amplifier offset, sensor nonlinearity, hysteresis, drift and calibration uncertainty. A 16-bit converter with a poor reference can be less accurate than a well-calibrated 12-bit device.

quiz.q: Distinguish a smart sensor from an intelligent instrument.
quiz.a: A smart sensor has its own processing and digital interface at chip or module level. An intelligent instrument is a complete panel meter or analyser with display, keypad and enclosure; it may contain a smart sensor inside.

quiz.q: A smart sensor reports 101.3 kPa on an I²C bus. List three internal checks you would want before trusting that number.
quiz.a: Check the self-calibration or reference reading, check the fault and status flags for open circuit, overrange or stuck output, and check the temperature compensation is active at the measured temperature. Also confirm the TEDS calibration date and range cover 101.3 kPa.

quiz.q: Name three digital buses used by smart sensors.
quiz.a: Any three of I²C, SPI, UART, CAN, and HART superimposed on a 4–20 mA loop.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial smart sensors are moving to IO-Link and wireless HART, where the TEDS travels with the device and a PLC reads it automatically. Research adds edge processing inside the sensor, so vibration or gas signatures are classified before the data leaves the chip. Digital twins use the same calibration memory to keep a simulation matched to the physical device. Search next for IEEE 1451 TEDS, IO-Link and HART.
